lines.speaker: Minos
lines.text: Right. This one — Sostratus, bandit — into the Pyriphlegethon. The temple-robber: to be torn apart by the Chimaera. The tyrant, Hermes, lay him out next to Tityus and let the vultures work on his liver as well. The rest of you — the decent ones — proceed promptly to the Elysian Fields and take up residence in the Isles of the Blessed, in recognition of your just conduct during life.
lines.description: brisk judicial sorting, dry docket-clearing authority

lines.speaker: Sostratus
lines.text: A moment, Minos. Hear me out — I think you'll find what I have to say is fair.

lines.speaker: Minos
lines.text: Hear you out? [sighs] Again? Sostratus, has it not already been established that you are a criminal who has killed a great many people?
lines.description: weary disbelief, bureaucrat dragged back into argument

lines.speaker: Sostratus
lines.text: Established, yes. But consider whether the punishment is also just.
lines.description: concedes neatly, setting the trap without haste

lines.speaker: Minos
lines.text: Entirely just — assuming it's just for a man to pay what he owes.
lines.description: firm, clipped, confident in the obvious ruling

lines.speaker: Sostratus
lines.text: Still — answer me one thing, Minos. It's a short question.

lines.speaker: Minos
lines.text: Be brief. There are others still to be sorted.
lines.description: impatient but controlled, eyes on the queue

lines.speaker: Sostratus
lines.text: Everything I did in life — was I doing it of my own free will, or was it spun out for me by Fate?
lines.description: measured, philosophical question with hidden steel

lines.speaker: Sostratus
lines.text: Then all of us — the ones called good and the ones called wicked — were simply carrying out her instructions when we did what we did?
lines.description: pressing gently, making the premise unavoidable

lines.speaker: Minos
lines.text: Yes. Clotho's instructions. She assigns each man his actions at birth.
lines.description: official explanation, still not seeing the corner

lines.speaker: Sostratus
lines.text: Now suppose somebody is forced by another to kill a man — unable to refuse the one compelling him. An executioner, say, obeying a judge; or a bodyguard, obeying a tyrant. Whom do you charge with the murder?

lines.speaker: Minos
lines.text: The judge, obviously. Or the tyrant. Not the sword either — the sword is just an instrument, serving the anger of the man who provided the original cause.

lines.speaker: Sostratus
lines.text: Excellent, Minos — you've actually improved on the example. And if a slave arrives carrying gold or silver, sent by his master — to whom is the gratitude owed? Whom does one record as the benefactor?
lines.description: pleased but restrained, enjoying the concession

lines.speaker: Minos
lines.text: The sender, Sostratus. The carrier was just the servant.
lines.description: matter-of-fact, a hint of suspicion dawning

lines.speaker: Sostratus
lines.text: Then do you see how unjustly you're behaving? Punishing us, who were the servants of Clotho's orders — and honouring these others, who were the servants of someone else's good deeds. Because nobody can claim it was possible to refuse, when the commands came down with absolute necessity.
lines.description: clear, triumphant logic; not smug, just exact

lines.speaker: Minos
lines.text: [long pause] Sostratus — you'd find a great many other things going on around here that don't quite stand up to scrutiny, if you looked at them closely. [pause] But here's what you've got out of your little cross-examination: it turns out you're not just a bandit — you're something of a sophist as well. Hermes, let him go. No further punishment. [sharply] And see that you don't teach the rest of the dead to ask the same questions.
lines.description: cornered, dry concession turning sharply managerial
